scenes.label: Set the scene for the 10-person simulation.
scenes.narration: Okay, now let's apply this theoretical framework to the dating story. Now imagine a society with 10 people, five men, five women, and all of them want to date and get married
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Set the scene for the 10-person simulation.

scenes.label: Establish the ranking criteria used to sort the five men.
scenes.narration: These five men will belong to five different social classes and will be ranked from 1 to 5 based on criteria such as appearance, health, wealth, and social status
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Establish the ranking criteria used to sort the five men.

scenes.label: Set up the top-vs-bottom rank contrast that drives the whole simulation.
scenes.narration:
Number five

will be the ultimate catch, while number one will be the lowest
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Set up the top-vs-bottom rank contrast that drives the whole simulation.

scenes.label: State the naive starting preference: everyone wants the top.
scenes.narration:
Instinctively, all women will want to marry number five, and all five men will want to marry all five women
at the same time
scenes.semanticTakeaway: State the naive starting preference: everyone wants the top.

scenes.label: Explain the underlying incentive on each side.
scenes.narration: This is because women want a partner who is capable of protecting and providing for them, while men want to maximize their fertility, so they want to date many women
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain the underlying incentive on each side.
scenes.semanticAction: the two incentives, face to face

scenes.label: Flag that the naive strategy breaks down — a quiet beat before the twist.
scenes.narration: However, if all the women only chase after number five, it won't work
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Flag that the naive strategy breaks down — a quiet beat before the twist.

scenes.label: Show the coalition that forms against the top-ranked man.
scenes.narration: Because the other four men will team up to deal with number five
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the coalition that forms against the top-ranked man.
scenes.semanticAction: four vs one at the table

scenes.label: First twist: being the most wanted backfires.
scenes.narration: If number five decides to date all five women at the same time, then number five will realize that number five is no longer the most desirable person
scenes.semanticTakeaway: First twist: being the most wanted backfires.

scenes.label: First domino of the cascade: girl 5 settles for guy 4.
scenes.narration: Because this guy is too promiscuous and doesn't guarantee a future for himself, the best option for girl number 5 at this point would be guy number 4
scenes.semanticTakeaway: First domino of the cascade: girl 5 settles for guy 4.

scenes.label: Second domino: the downgrade keeps propagating.
scenes.narration: At this point, girl number 4 will lose her best option, so she'll have to choose guy number 3
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Second domino: the downgrade keeps propagating.

scenes.label: Compress the rest of the cascade into one beat.
scenes.narration: Then girl number 3 will have to marry guy number 2. And girl number 2 will marry guy number 1
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Compress the rest of the cascade into one beat.

scenes.label: Land the cascade's punchline: the top-ranked man ends up worst off.
scenes.narration: And the result is that guy number 5, the most eager one, ends up stuck with girl number 1
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Land the cascade's punchline: the top-ranked man ends up worst off.

scenes.label: Give the model a caveat, then move on — a breathing beat after the twist.
scenes.narration: Actually, girl number 3 could still marry guy number 5 because the difference between 5 and 2 is quite large. But to simplify, let's just assume the above
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Give the model a caveat, then move on — a breathing beat after the twist.

scenes.label: Summarize who won and lost in the naive strategy.
scenes.narration: And the final result is that guy number 5, who should have gotten the best result, gets the worst result. All the girls get worse results than they should have, except for girl number 1. The only good thing is that all the guys benefit
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Summarize who won and lost in the naive strategy.

scenes.label: State the general principle the toy example illustrates.
scenes.narration: Actually, this is just a small assumption to illustrate the point: in a game, the strongest person who is too greedy will suffer a bitter end, and their rivals will be the ones who benefit directly
scenes.semanticTakeaway: State the general principle the toy example illustrates.

scenes.label: Answer who actually wins in the long run.
scenes.narration: From this, we can deduce that the strongest person isn't the one who can steal everything from everyone else, but the one who can coordinate so that everyone benefits the most
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Answer who actually wins in the long run.

scenes.label: Contrast short-term vs long-term payoff of greed.
scenes.narration: Because if they just steal, the strongest person might win in the short term, but in the long term, everyone will lose
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Contrast short-term vs long-term payoff of greed.
scenes.semanticAction: short vs long term at the boardroom

scenes.label: Show the unequal pairing still has friction.
scenes.narration: Because even though Mr. Four gets Ms. Five, there's still a disparity between the two, so conflicts and difficulties will inevitably arise
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the unequal pairing still has friction.

scenes.label: Resolve the simulation: cooperation beats competition.
scenes.narration: Therefore, the best solution is cooperation. Mr. Five takes Ms. Five, Mr. Four takes Ms. Four, Mr. Three takes Ms. Three – everyone finds a partner, everyone has children, and society develops
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Resolve the simulation: cooperation beats competition.

scenes.label: Name the concept the simulation just demonstrated.
scenes.narration: This state — game theory calls it Nash equilibrium. This is a state where no one benefits more from unilaterally changing strategies. It's like everyone is happy, and any change would only lead to more losses.
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the concept the simulation just demonstrated.

paperCards.title: Nash Equilibrium
paperCards.body: This state — game theory calls it Nash equilibrium. This is a state where no one benefits more from unilaterally changing strategies. It's like everyone is happy, and any change would only lead to more losses.

scenes.label: Break the toy model's scale assumption — the real complication.
scenes.narration: So, let's just keep things as they are. Okay. That theory is perfectly fine. But there's a problem: society doesn't just have 10 people, but 8 billion people. So, there's...
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Break the toy model's scale assumption — the real complication.

scenes.label: Introduce a real-world survey to test the theory against reality.
scenes.narration: A fun survey asks: If you're 30 years old, your parents are pressuring you to get married, you've been dating for 10 years and haven't found anyone you like, and now you're forced to get married, what are your minimum requirements for agreeing to marry someone
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Introduce a real-world survey to test the theory against reality.

paperCards.title: Survey: your minimum requirement?

scenes.label: Show the gendered asymmetry in the survey answers.
scenes.narration: I think it would be simpler for guys. Like, any girl will do, even girl number one would be fine. Some girls say that if I don't love that guy now, if I don't find him attractive, then at least he must be earning around 200 million a month
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the gendered asymmetry in the survey answers.

scenes.label: Show theory (equilibrium) failing against real preference.
scenes.narration: According to Nash equilibrium, number three should marry number three and live happily. But in reality, number three will look at number three and think, "It's better to stay single
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show theory (equilibrium) failing against real preference.

scenes.label: Give the holdout her exact bar — nobody but the top or a huge income.
scenes.narration: Unless I meet number five or he earns 200 million a month, then I won't consider it. Because there's no reason to suffer by getting involved with someone who's on par with me, risking having to be on par with him and then having to cater to him
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Give the holdout her exact bar — nobody but the top or a huge income.

scenes.label: Show the real-world version of everyone chasing #5.
scenes.narration: In reality, many people rush into the top 1-2%, and most end up being left behind. For example, Elon Musk, he has a ton of children and many wives. Billionaires and celebrities have no shortage of people lining up for them
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the real-world version of everyone chasing #5.

scenes.label: Full-bleed emotional beat: the human cost of involuntary singlehood — no character, let the image sit.
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, many young people around the world are also experiencing the situation of being involuntarily single. That is, they want a partner, they want to get married, but they can't
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Full-bleed emotional beat: the human cost of involuntary singlehood — no character, let the image sit.

scenes.label: Show what giving up looks like for young men specifically.
scenes.narration: So gradually, they give up. As for the guys, they'd rather stay home playing games, browsing the internet, and watching movies. So, many young men in their 25s and 30s have never dated, never had a relationship, and don't want to try anymore
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show what giving up looks like for young men specifically.
scenes.semanticAction: cat withdrawing to a screen at home

scenes.label: Host breaks the fourth wall — self-deprecating breather beat.
scenes.narration: Grandpa, that sounds like me, right? It's not because they're ugly or incompetent, but simply because the dating game now is too tiring. The competition is fierce, and the probability of winning is low
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Host breaks the fourth wall — self-deprecating breather beat.

scenes.label: Recap: players and rules are unchanged — sets up the reveal that the reward changed.
scenes.narration: That's the theory that says balancing things out is the optimal approach. But in reality, people don't want to play that game anymore. Why? As I said, in a game there are three parts: the players. This hasn't changed much. The rules of the game are competition, and that hasn't changed much.
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Recap: players and rules are unchanged — sets up the reveal that the reward changed.

scenes.label: Pose the reward question directly.
scenes.narration: The final thing is the reward. It seems that the rewards of dating in modern times have changed somewhat. Usually, we think of dating rewards as love, sex, marriage, and having children. But now there's another very important element
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Pose the reward question directly.

scenes.label: Name the new reward: social status.
scenes.narration: It was important in the past, but now it's exaggerated a lot. It's social status, meaning your reputation and your position in the eyes of others
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the new reward: social status.

scenes.label: Frame the new test for a relationship: can you show it off?
scenes.narration: Simply put, if you love this person and marry this person, can you show them off
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Frame the new test for a relationship: can you show it off?

scenes.label: Enumerate the specific show-off venues.
scenes.narration: Can you be proud in the eyes of others? Can you show them off on Facebook? Can you show them off on Instagram? Can you show them off at a class reunion and brag about how handsome and rich your husband is, or how hot and capable your wife is? Now, the story has added an extremely important element: reputation
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Enumerate the specific show-off venues.

scenes.label: Show the same show-off logic beyond marriage.
scenes.narration: And it doesn't just stop at marriage. It also manifests in things like the latest iPhone, luxurious travel and check-ins, and buying designer goods. Many people do things not because they actually use them, but because they want to show off
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the same show-off logic beyond marriage.

scenes.label: Land the consequence: marrying beneath your image is embarrassing.
scenes.narration: And marriage is also part of this game. If you marry someone who isn't worthy, it will be embarrassing. So it's better to be single than to marry someone who doesn't meet the standards.
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Land the consequence: marrying beneath your image is embarrassing.

scenes.label: Name the mechanism that makes this reward so brutal: zero-sum.
scenes.narration: The scary thing is that the game of showing off is a zero-sum game. That means there will always be people better and people worse off. If everyone could show off, then no one would be able to show off
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the mechanism that makes this reward so brutal: zero-sum.

scenes.label: Show why zero-sum means someone must always lose.
scenes.narration: Because if everyone showed off, then no one would be. If there are people at the top, there must be people at the bottom
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show why zero-sum means someone must always lose.

scenes.label: Callback to the opening: explain why cash incentives fail — money alone, sitting unused.
scenes.narration: There are many opinions that the government of various countries giving money to people to encourage having children is ineffective. Because the problem isn't a lack of money
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Callback to the opening: explain why cash incentives fail — money alone, sitting unused.

scenes.label: Rule out the 'no jobs' explanation.
scenes.narration: Nowadays, finding a job is easier. I know there's a lot of unemployment now, but it's easier than in the past. In the past, people only knew how to work in the fields. Now there are more choices. So now, people can find a normal job, be healthy, and at least earn enough to live on
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Rule out the 'no jobs' explanation.

scenes.label: State the video's core thesis line.
scenes.narration: But the important thing is that people lack face. And face can't necessarily be bought with money
scenes.semanticTakeaway: State the video's core thesis line.

scenes.label: Test the thesis with a concrete hypothetical.
scenes.narration: If you give people 1 billion to force them to marry someone their friends look down on, what meaning does that 1 billion have? Actually, it does have meaning, but in the end
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Test the thesis with a concrete hypothetical.

scenes.label: Confirm: money alone doesn't close the deal.
scenes.narration: In those cases, some people would rather not marry a billion dollars than have to get married
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Confirm: money alone doesn't close the deal.

scenes.label: Pivot question into the historical-stages section.
scenes.narration: Here's a question: why do humans always chase after this kind of "face" while our species has survived for tens of thousands of years, remaining very numerous and not becoming extinct? The answer is:
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Pivot question into the historical-stages section.

scenes.label: Credit the source video/creator this analysis is adapted from.
scenes.narration: From Mr. Giang in the Preditive History channel, it's that humans didn't behave like that before because the game has changed over time. Game theory has a concept called the overall picture of society, that is, the big context surrounding the game
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Credit the source video/creator this analysis is adapted from.

scenes.label: Name the context variables that define which game gets played.
scenes.narration: Specifically in this case, it's the population size, whether society is rich or poor, whether there are external enemies, how advanced the technology is. These factors combine to determine which game is played. When the context changes, the game changes too
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the context variables that define which game gets played.

scenes.label: Set up the three-act historical structure (Chekhov's gun — paid off at the China/Korea/Vietnam sections).
scenes.narration: Now, let's divide human history into three stages for easier understanding
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Set up the three-act historical structure (Chekhov's gun — paid off at the China/Korea/Vietnam sections).

scenes.label: Establish stage 1's harsh conditions.
scenes.narration: The first stage is the primitive era. A small village at that time had only about 200 people. Everything was inconvenient and scarce. People had to defecate in the fields, sometimes even getting bitten by snakes. And to get clean water, they had to carry it home and boil it before drinking
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Establish stage 1's harsh conditions.

scenes.label: Land how dangerous childbirth was in this era.
scenes.narration: Having children in such circumstances was like stepping into a death trap
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Land how dangerous childbirth was in this era.

scenes.label: Show stage 1's reproduction strategy: no romance, communal parenting logic.
scenes.narration: In that context, there was no concept of love or dating; women and men would have many lovers at the same time, firstly to increase the chances of reproduction for everyone, and secondly to avoid knowing whose child was whose
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show stage 1's reproduction strategy: no romance, communal parenting logic.

texts.content: No love. No dating. Just survival.

scenes.label: Explain the payoff of this strategy: communal child protection.
scenes.narration: When the men in the village all thought the child might be theirs, everyone would flock together to protect and care for it. And the reward would be ensuring the entire village didn't become extinct
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain the payoff of this strategy: communal child protection.
scenes.semanticAction: the whole village protecting a child

scenes.label: Mark the scale jump into stage 2.
scenes.narration: Let's move on to the second stage, when the small village started to expand into a society of tens of thousands of people. At this point, there was money coming in and going out, and some rudimentary technology
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Mark the scale jump into stage 2.

scenes.label: Show stage 2's defining condition: constant warfare.
scenes.narration: At this time, villages, communes, and tribes began fighting each other incessantly to compete for territory and resources. Therefore, society became extremely short of people
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show stage 2's defining condition: constant warfare.

scenes.label: Explain why there was no time for courtship in stage 2 — a wartime establishing shot.
scenes.narration: Because there was a need for soldiers to go to war, and people to work in the fields. In such a chaotic situation, where would they find the time for courtship and romantic dates
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain why there was no time for courtship in stage 2 — a wartime establishing shot.

scenes.label: Show the resulting institution: arranged marriage by parents.
scenes.narration: And so, arranged marriages took center stage. Parents decided where their children were, with no room for argument. At this point, whether the child was born or not, whether they liked it or not, didn't matter, as long as they got married and had many children
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the resulting institution: arranged marriage by parents.

scenes.label: Arrive at stage 3 (today) with the scale that makes cooperation hard again.
scenes.narration: And finally, the third stage is the present day. Now the world is crowded, with 8 billion people. Look at China or India, each country has over 1 billion people, very crowded
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Arrive at stage 3 (today) with the scale that makes cooperation hard again.

scenes.label: Show stage 3's inequality alongside its wealth.
scenes.narration: And there's much more money too. But some people have more than enough while others struggle to make ends meet, which is very unequal
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show stage 3's inequality alongside its wealth.
scenes.semanticAction: rich vs struggling at the counter

scenes.label: Give stage 3 its genuine upside: safer childbirth.
scenes.narration: The upside is that healthcare is better, technology is more advanced, so women who give birth are almost guaranteed to survive, reducing the risk of childbirth being a death sentence
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Give stage 3 its genuine upside: safer childbirth.

scenes.label: Full-bleed beat: a relatively peaceful modern skyline, no war of stage 2.
scenes.narration:
And then, the world is relatively peaceful in a certain way.

The superpowers no longer directly shoot each other with guns, but instead wage proxy wars
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Full-bleed beat: a relatively peaceful modern skyline, no war of stage 2.

scenes.label: Bridge from 'life is better' to 'so expectations rose too'.
scenes.narration: Or, if they just talk big, life would be much better. But because life is better, people expect dating to be good too
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Bridge from 'life is better' to 'so expectations rose too'.

scenes.label: Set up the tradeoff logic used in the next beat.
scenes.narration: While dating, falling in love, and marriage, like everything else, must have both good and bad aspects
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Set up the tradeoff logic used in the next beat.

scenes.label: Explain the modern logic of dating up instead of at your level.
scenes.narration: So if you have to endure hardship, why date someone from the same social class and suffer together? Why not choose someone from a higher social class? So now, dating is pretty much like a jump-starting platform
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain the modern logic of dating up instead of at your level.

scenes.label: Name the concrete apps that formalize this jump-up logic.
scenes.narration:
Low-level clouds try to climb to higher levels. Apps like Tinder, Bumble, or Facebook Ding are essentially platforms where people
try to find a better match to jump to
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the concrete apps that formalize this jump-up logic.

scenes.label: Show the logical trap: if everyone aims up, no one accepts their level — a crowded street of climbers.
scenes.narration: But the problem is, if everyone wants to jump to a higher level, who will want to marry someone at their own level
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the logical trap: if everyone aims up, no one accepts their level — a crowded street of climbers.

scenes.label: Callback to the earlier cast (level 3 wanting level 5).
scenes.narration:
It's like,
being at level three but wanting to be at level five, or at most level four, because if you say you're at level three like yourself, then just stay put
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Callback to the earlier cast (level 3 wanting level 5).
scenes.semanticAction: girl3 at the bar, aiming up

scenes.label: Land the consequence and the collapse warning.
scenes.narration: So, marriage and childbirth are plummeting. And Mr. Giang says that if this trend continues, society will collapse sooner or later
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Land the consequence and the collapse warning.

And according to him, history

scenes.label: Introduce the replacement birth rate benchmark.
scenes.narration: Speaking of collapse, let's look at the numbers. Currently, the replacement birth rate is 2.1 children per woman. That means a mother has to give birth to at least two children for the population to remain at its current level
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Introduce the replacement birth rate benchmark.

scenes.label: Lay out the danger thresholds below replacement rate.
scenes.narration: Below 2.1, we start seeing a shortage of people. Below 1.5, the decline is rapid. If it drops below 1.0, then society is essentially self-destructing
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Lay out the danger thresholds below replacement rate.

scenes.label: Show the positive-contrast side of the map first: Africa's high birth rate.
scenes.narration: Looking at the world map, we see it's divided into two states: in Africa, people still have very high birth rates. In some regions, each mother gives birth to five to seven children
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the positive-contrast side of the map first: Africa's high birth rate.

scenes.label: Explain why: survival and territory competition still reward more children.
scenes.narration: Because there, they are still in the stage where they need people to survive and then fight for territory and things like that, so they just have as many children as possible to compensate
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain why: survival and territory competition still reward more children.

scenes.label: Contrast with the falling side of the map.
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, in the wealthy regions of North America, Europe, and East Asia, the birth rate is plummeting. In North America and Europe, there are still immigrants; if native women don't want to have children, then so be it
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Contrast with the falling side of the map.

scenes.label: Show the West's solution: immigration.
scenes.narration: They will open their doors to foreigners to work, pay taxes, and contribute to the economy. But it also causes a lot of headaches in terms of culture and politics
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the West's solution: immigration.

scenes.label: Pivot to East Asia, which lacks the immigration option.

scenes.label: Explain why immigration isn't a fix in East Asia's closed culture.

Because here, there's no such thing as easily opening the doors to immigrants.
Because East Asian culture is quite closed, it's very difficult to accept complete strangers and have them sit at the same table
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Explain why immigration isn't a fix in East Asia's closed culture.

scenes.label: Introduce South Korea's world-lowest birth rate.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Introduce South Korea's world-lowest birth rate.

scenes.label: State the demographic endpoint plainly.
scenes.narration: With this population, South Korea will probably only survive for a few more generations before disappearing from the map
scenes.semanticTakeaway: State the demographic endpoint plainly.

scenes.label: Concrete cultural evidence: 'no kid zones'.
scenes.narration: Now, there are even restaurants there with signs saying "no kids allowed," a so-called "no kid zone." It's as if they consider children to be a nuisance, noisy, and ruining the experience for other customers
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Concrete cultural evidence: 'no kid zones'.

scenes.label: Name the cultural driver: extreme appearance standards.
scenes.narration: According to Mr. Giang, South Korea is like that because it's a society that values ​​appearances to an extreme degree. Everything has to be beautiful, high-quality, and expensive
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Name the cultural driver: extreme appearance standards.

scenes.label: Give a concrete example of the perfection standard: showbiz idols.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Give a concrete example of the perfection standard: showbiz idols.

scenes.label: Show the narrow binary path to success in Korea.
scenes.narration: And because of that, the path to success there is quite narrow. Either you get into a prestigious university and work for Samsung or some other big corporation, or you have no decent options at all
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the narrow binary path to success in Korea.

scenes.label: Quantify the economic argument against having multiple kids.
scenes.narration: So, if you're a middle-class family in Korea, you'll hear this economic argument: If you have three children, you need more than three times the money and resources
scenes.semanticTakeaway: Quantify the economic argument against having multiple kids.

scenes.label: Show the resulting strategy: all resources into one child.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Show the resulting strategy: all resources into one child.

scenes.label: State the endpoint of that logic.
scenes.narration: And this logic forces people to only dare to have one child, or to just stop having children altogether to avoid the burden
scenes.semanticTakeaway: State the endpoint of that logic.

scenes.label: Project the demographic timeline forward.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Project the demographic timeline forward.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Land the workforce collapse figure.

scenes.label: Visualize the endpoint: an economy of retirees only.

scenes.semanticTakeaway: Visualize the endpoint: an economy of retirees only.
